passages.t: A woman with no children, and her rival
passages.happening:
The book opens with one family. Elkanah, a man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim, has two wives. “And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none” (verse 2).

“Year after year Elkanah would go up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts at Shiloh, where Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests to the LORD” (verse 3). At the feast he hands out portions of the meat to Peninnah and all her children. “But to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved her even though the LORD had closed her womb” (verse 5).

Peninnah uses Hannah's childlessness against her. ‘Her rival would provoke her and taunt her viciously’ (verse 6), and it happens every year. Hannah weeps and will not eat (verse 7).

“Hannah, why are you crying?” her husband Elkanah asked. “Why won’t you eat? Why is your heart so grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
These are the last years of the judges, probably in the eleventh century BC. Israel has no king and no capital. Its main sanctuary is at Shiloh, about twenty miles north of Jerusalem in the land of Ephraim, where the ark of the covenant had been kept since the days of Joshua. The chapter calls it the house and temple of the LORD, so by now there seems to have been a building there as well as the tent.

In that world a woman's security and standing depended on bearing children, above all sons, who carried on the family name and cared for their parents in old age. Being childless was painful and shaming, and people often took it as a sign that God was displeased. A man whose first wife had no children might take a second, and the Bible's stories of such homes, Abraham's and Jacob's among them, are full of rivalry and grief. The word for Peninnah, rival, is the word for a second wife in the same house.

The yearly sacrifice was a family feast. Part of the offering was burned for the LORD, part went to the priest, and the family ate the rest. That is why Elkanah hands out portions. Each year the meal sets out in public who has children and who has none, and each year Peninnah presses on the wound.

Elkanah loves Hannah, and his double portion shows it. His question is kind, and it misses her completely. He answers her sorrow by pointing to himself.

The title the LORD of Hosts appears here for the first time in the Bible. The hosts are armies, of heaven and of Israel, and the title presents the LORD as commander of every power. It is to this God that a grieving woman will bring her prayer.

One more detail carries a warning. The priests there are Hophni and Phinehas, Eli's sons. They are named in verse 3 and say nothing yet. The next chapter will show what they are.
passages.later:
Israel's story is full of women who waited for children, and God remembered each of them. Rachel, the wife Jacob loved more, cried, “Give me children, or I will die!” (Genesis 30:1). A psalm praises the God who “settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children” (Psalm 113:9).

In the New Testament Elizabeth waits until old age, and when her son is coming she says that God has taken away ‘my disgrace among the people’ (Luke 1:25).
passages.hard:
‘The LORD had closed her womb’ (verses 5 and 6). Does God punish people with childlessness? And was Hannah being punished?

The text says twice that the LORD had closed Hannah's womb, and later that the LORD remembered her (verse 19). The Old Testament speaks this way because it holds that life and its beginning are in God's hands. That does not make Hannah's suffering simple. It means her story is not ruled by chance, or by her rival.

What the text does not say matters as much. It never says that Hannah had sinned or that God was angry with her. Nothing in the chapter blames her. The people around her may have read her childlessness as a sign of God's displeasure, but the narrator does not. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah were all childless for years, and none of them is blamed for it. The rest of the Bible refuses to turn childlessness into a verdict on any one person.

A word of care. This story ends in joy for one couple. It does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Elkanah loved Hannah and still asked the wrong question. Ask whether there is someone near you whose grief you have answered with a reason why they should feel better. And if you are the one who cannot eat at the feast, ask who you could let into that grief, and whether you have told God what it is really like.

passages.happening:
After the meal Hannah stands up. Eli the priest is sitting on a chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD (verse 9). “In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears” (verse 10).

She makes a vow. “O LORD of Hosts, if only You will look upon the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, not forgetting Your maidservant but giving her a son, then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever come over his head” (verse 11).

She prays in her heart. Her lips move, but no sound comes. Eli watches her mouth and thinks she is drunk. “How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine!” (verse 14).

“No, my lord,” Hannah replied. “I am a woman oppressed in spirit. I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD” (verse 15). She asks him not to take her for a wicked woman, for she has been praying ‘out of the depth of my anguish and grief’ (verse 16).

“Go in peace,” Eli replied, “and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him” (verse 17). Hannah goes on her way. She eats again, ‘and her face was no longer downcast’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Praying aloud was normal in the ancient world. A woman praying with moving lips and no voice was unusual enough that the priest misread her. The scene is full of irony. The priest of God's house cannot tell prayer from drink, and in the next chapter his own sons will be found treating the LORD's offering with contempt.

Hannah's vow has a condition: if God gives her a son, she will give him back. The words ‘no razor shall ever come over his head’ recall the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, a special setting apart to God that was usually taken for a set time. Hannah makes it for her son's whole life, as was said of Samson before his birth. Israel's law took vows seriously, and it allowed a husband to confirm or cancel his wife's vow (Numbers 30). Elkanah will let hers stand.

Her prayer is not tidy. She speaks of her affliction and asks God to look and to remember. The chapter calls it pouring out her soul. She brings her grief to God instead of hiding it, and the text honors that.

Notice when her face changes. Eli's words are a prayer for her, not yet an answer. Nothing in her body has changed. But she has given her grief to God, and she can eat again.

The verb to ask runs through the whole chapter. Hannah asks, Eli prays that God will grant what she asked, and soon she will name her son because she asked for him. In Hebrew the word asked for is spelled like the name Saul, and many readers hear in it a quiet hint of the king Israel will ask for later in the book.
passages.later:
The psalms invite the same honest prayer: “Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge” (Psalm 62:8).

Luke's Gospel opens with a story built on this one. An old couple has no child, a promise is made at the house of God, and the boy is to be set apart from birth: “He shall never take wine or strong drink” (Luke 1:15).
passages.asks: Hannah prayed out of the depth of her anguish, and a priest thought she was drunk. Ask whether you have ever misjudged someone's pain because it did not look the way you expected. And ask whether you have poured out your own soul before the LORD, or only said the words you thought he wanted.

passages.happening:
The next morning the family worships and goes home to Ramah. Elkanah lies with Hannah, ‘and the LORD remembered her’ (verse 19). In time Hannah gives birth to a son. She names him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD” (verse 20).

When the family next goes up to Shiloh, Hannah stays behind. She will bring the boy once he is weaned, ‘to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently’ (verse 22). “Do what you think is best,” her husband Elkanah replied, “and stay here until you have weaned him” (verse 23).

When the boy is weaned, Hannah takes him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour and a skin of wine. ‘Though the boy was still young’, she brings him to Eli (verses 24-25).

“Please, my lord,” said Hannah, “as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD. I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, I now dedicate the boy to the LORD” (verses 26-28). ‘So they worshiped the LORD there’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
‘The LORD remembered her.’ In the Bible, when God remembers someone, it does not mean he had forgotten. It means he acts for them, as when he remembered Noah in the flood and Rachel in her longing for a child.

Children were weaned much later then than now, often at two or three years old. So Samuel is still very small when Hannah brings him to Shiloh. He will live there in the care of the priest, at the nation's main sanctuary.

The gifts are generous: a bull, a large measure of flour, and wine. Hannah comes to give thanks, and she gives freely.

The verb to ask comes back at the end. Hannah says that the LORD granted what she asked, and then she gives the boy to the LORD for as long as he lives. The word translated dedicate is a form of the same verb, meaning something like given on request or lent. She asked God for a son, and now she gives him back.

There is another irony here, and some readers see it as part of the point. The child is left in the house of Eli, whose own sons are corrupt. God will keep him there.
passages.later:
Luke tells of a later child brought to the house of the LORD by his parents. When Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem, ‘to present Him to the Lord’ (Luke 2:22), the scene recalls Hannah bringing Samuel to Shiloh.

And when John the Baptist is born, his relatives ask, “What then will this child become?” (Luke 1:66), the question asked about the children God gave by his special gift in the Old Testament, Samuel among them.
passages.hard:
How could a mother give away her young child? And was it right to make such a vow?

To modern readers, leaving a small child at a sanctuary can sound like abandonment. The text presents it differently. Samuel is placed in the care of the high priest at the nation's main shrine, a place of honor, and Hannah goes on visiting him every year with a robe she has made (2:19). Parents in that world often apprenticed children young, and giving a child to a sanctuary was a known, if rare, practice.

The story does not pretend it was easy. Hannah's vow costs her the son she longed for, and the narrator honors her for keeping it.

The chapter does not tell parents to do what Hannah did. It describes a costly act of faith, in which a woman gives back to God the gift she most wanted. It is not a pattern for parents today.
passages.asks: Hannah gave back the very gift she had asked for. Ask what good gift in your life you hold most tightly, and what it would mean to hold it as belonging to God. And ask how you thank God when a prayer is answered, whether with words only, or with something it costs you to give.
